name: Orokaiva
catalog_quote: The first syllable of each Orokaiva word is stressed. When h occurs between unstressed vowels it is very light, and sometimes seems to be quite silent.

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on printed p.34 of the held PL-A18 scan (page image inspected). (2) The deciding source is a 1969 preliminary grammar sketch from two weeks' fieldwork; the best available stress description is Larsen & Larsen 1977, a dedicated SIL phonology from 28 months' fieldwork, which I fetched sources from the Wayback copy of the old SIL PNG site and scanned. Its sec. 5.1 (p.12) states 'Stress is non-phonemic. The primary stress is always on the first syllable of each word', i.e. it independently confirms fixed initial stress (our 'fixed-strict', rule 10 100 1000...), and refines with secondary stress on the third syllable of simple words / first syllable of second root in compounds, near-equal prominence of syllable 2 in initial Va sequences, and lengthening of stressed vowels. sources.quote: "The first syllable of each Orokaiva word is stressed." (Healey, Isoroembo & Chittleborough 1969, p. 34)

sources.citation: Larsen, Robert & Marlys Larsen. 1977. Orokaiva phonology and orthography. In Richard Loving (ed.), Phonologies of five P.N.G. languages (Workpapers in Papua New Guinea Languages 19), 5-28. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics.
sources.quote: "Stress is non-phonemic. The primary stress is always on the first syllable of each word. If the first two syllables involve the sequence Va, then the second syllable sometimes seems to be nearly as prominent as the first one. In reduplicated and compound words a secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of the second root. In simple words a secondary stress tends to occur on the third syllable, but it is not easily heard if that syllable does not contain a stop or /a/." Also p.12 sec. 5.2: "Vowels in monosyllables and stressed syllables tend to be lengthened."
sources.note: The only dedicated phonology of Orokaiva (Glottolog hhtype 'phonology'); our coding rested on a 1969 two-week preliminary sketch. fetched sources now; p.12 confirms initial primary stress and adds secondary-stress detail.
